One of this year’s most joyous French adult animated comedies, Jim Queen, which blew away Cannes and inspired the most raucous screening in Annecy history, according to artistic director Marcel Jean, will get a U.S. release after being picked up by Magnolia Pictures, which is planning an English-language theatrical release for next summer.

The acquisition was announced earlier today by Deadline.

Directed by Marco Nguyen and Nicolas Athané, Jim Queen was produced by French animation studio Bobbypills and Belgium’s Umedia, with animation from Bobbypills, Réunion-based Gao Shan Pictures, and Belgium’s Studio Waooh!. The film follows a muscular gay influencer whose celebrity status evaporates when a mysterious virus begins turning gay men straight. With the help of his devoted admirer Lucien, Jim sets out across Paris’s gay nightlife scene in search of a cure.

The irreverent, vibrant comedy world premiered in Cannes’ Midnight Screenings section, where it was well received by critics and laypeople, praised for its unapologetically queer humor and provocative premise. Variety critic Guy Lodge described it as a queer South Park on steroids.

The film’s English-language dub stars Jordan Firstman (I Love LA, Rotting in the Sun) as the film’s titular lead, alongside comedian Matteo Lane as Lucien. The supporting voice cast includes Nicole Byer, John Cameron Mitchell, Bob the Drag Queen, and Wendie Malick.

The acquisition gives one of this year’s most celebrated festival films a theatrical foothold in the U.S., where adult-oriented independent animation remains a relatively rare presence on the big screen.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is 18 Months, directed by Paulo Garcia and Natália Gouvea and produced by Zombie Studio. Based on the true story of two men who became parents after a baby was found in a New York subway, the film combines stop-motion puppets and miniature sets with projected 2D animation and digital facial expressions. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning the Grand Jury Award at Animayo Gran Canaria 2026.

Shifts in scale and technique convey the emotional uncertainty of Pete and Danny’s unlikely path to parenthood. A judge casts an oversized shadow over the process, representing the legal system’s tremendous weight, while background characters appear as disproportionate silhouettes projected directly onto handmade sets. By synchronizing those projections with the stop-motion animation, artists could work with both elements together and make real the pressures that surround the couple as they navigate an often difficult situation.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Paulo Garcia and Natália Gouvea: What first moved us was the extraordinary true story of a baby found in a New York subway, and Pete and Danny’s decision to embrace him as their own. Their journey reminds us what love means in its purest form: unconditional, courageous, and transformative. They raised that child into a wonderful young man, despite society’s prejudices. At a time when hard-won LGBTQ+ rights are increasingly challenged, we felt this story needed to be told. Because a family is not defined by its structure, but by the love that holds it together. And love should never need permission.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film?

Our greatest responsibility was honoring Pete and Danny’s real story, portraying their emotions with enough sensitivity that they could recognize themselves in our animated world. We discovered how every detail could become storytelling, from words about prejudice and love embedded in the walls to cinematography bringing miniature New York to life. Then came the beautiful chaos of stop motion. We spent hours debating how Pete should move while floating through a vortex, watching his baby being taken away. Should he swim? Drift? How could movement express such helplessness? We learned that directing means embracing uncertainty while keeping hundreds of talented artists inspired.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Natália and I have fallen increasingly in love with stop motion. It combines animation’s imagination with the visual richness of live-action filmmaking. For 18 Months, we wanted something tangible, intimate, and emotionally grounded, with New York becoming another character. Budgetary limitations also inspired creative solutions. Secondary characters became 2D animal silhouettes projected onto physical sets, transforming society into shadows surrounding Pete and Danny. In the courtroom, an oversized judge puppet embodied the overwhelming weight of justice. Each technique served an emotional purpose. Ultimately, we wanted the animation to make this extraordinary true story feel even more human.

What was the biggest technical challenge in combining stop motion, projection, and digital animation into a cohesive film?

Our biggest challenge was integrating projections directly on set rather than in post-production. Synchronizing the projector with Dragonframe allowed every frame to capture both the puppets and animated silhouettes, giving animators real-time references. Cinematography had to carefully balance physical lighting with the projections. Facial expressions presented another challenge. Given our production scale and puppet limitations, we animated them digitally, requiring meticulous lighting references and mapping to integrate them seamlessly into the footage. The goal was always to make these different techniques disappear into one believable world, allowing audiences to focus entirely on the characters and their emotions.

Sony Pictures Classics has released the U.S. trailer for Louis Clichy’s Iron Boy, one of the year’s most acclaimed animated features and one of this award season’s strongest international contenders.

The hand-drawn film will open in New York and Los Angeles on December 4 for an awards-qualifying run before expanding nationwide on January 22, 2027.

Since premiering at Cannes, Iron Boy has put together an impressive collection of prestige festival honors, including the Special Jury Prize in the Un Certain Regard section, both the jury and audience awards for best feature at Annecy, and two more prizes at Animation Is Film, including the audience award.

Set in rural France, the film follows 11-year-old Christophe, whose life on his family’s farm is upended when a medical condition forces him to wear a rigid iron corset, hence the title. His adjustment, which takes on a fantastic element at times, opens the door to new friendships, music, and an identity beyond his well-meaning father’s expectations.

The film’s striking, deceptively simple ink-and-watercolor aesthetic is a radical departure for Clichy, a Hollywood vet whose previous credits include Pixar’s Wall-E and Up and two CG Asterix features.

In our Annecy interview, the filmmaker talked us through the film’s deeply personal origins, its unconventional production, and his determination to prioritize expressive animation over polished detail.

“Is the animation industry doing enough for people of color?” Framing the question already suggests an answer, and that answer is no. But where do we go from here? How can the industry remove the roadblocks preventing people of color from thriving, and is breaking away from mainstream studios the only way forward?

In one of the highlights of this year’s Manchester Animation Festival industry program, three U.K. panelists gathered to discuss the representation of people of color in positions of power within the British animation industry and beyond. The discussion was moderated by London-based writer and Cartoon Brew contributor Ryan Gaur.

The following report draws on the wide-ranging, 80-minute discussion.

Advocating For Creative Access

“The hiring bias is endemic in the animation industry,” says talent development and inclusion expert Rico Johnson-Sinclair. “On one hand, there’s external pressure on organizations to hire more historically marginalized people, but the reality is that it ends up with people stuck in entry-level jobs because there’s no one to invest in them. And that’s largely because there aren’t enough people in positions of power to be able to advocate for different voices in the medium.”

For Amy Ashton, co-founder and director of BlackFrame, a newly launched initiative that amplifies Black talent in animation, it’s also about questioning the motivations behind these decisions.

“I’ve been advocating for creative access for 12 years now, and I have seen a kind of stagnation in the lack of representation. People do get opportunities to take the next step, but whether companies are implementing these schemes in the right way remains questionable. I think the question we need to ask is what is the intention behind it, because that has to be in the right place.”

Raised on movies, video games, and comics of the 1980s, Michael Morgan has been navigating the industry for almost 20 years. As a senior animator, mentor, and internationally experienced artist, he’s repeatedly witnessed the gap between representation at universities and within studios.

“When you get to the studios, sometimes even if there’s about a thousand people, I can count on my hands how many Black people there are, a few Asians as well, but not many. And at the supervisor level, it’s very low as well.”

Debunking A Common Myth

For all three panelists, hiring bias and the lack of representation extend well beyond the animation industry. But these problems are also directly connected to the common misconception that talent from underrepresented communities is difficult to find. That perception was one of the reasons Ashton co-founded BlackFrame in the first place.

“It started as a way to attract these talents, but also to build a database for that community,” she explains. “Our very first event was sold out, and even among the attendees, the conclusion was: we’re actually all here. I think it’s time to address industry people and people in positions of power, opening their eyes. But then again, it’s a fine line to navigate because on the one hand, you want to broaden exposure to talent, but on the other hand, you don’t want to be (or feel) hired because of your identity.”

For Johnson-Sinclair, that misconception also stems from studios and organizations being reluctant to adapt, instead focusing on finding people who fit into their established systems. That, in turn, provides an excuse to avoid rethinking their structures, coaching programs, and initiatives to better accommodate underrepresented talent.

The Bigger Picture Behind The Screen

To enter the industry and build a sustainable career, Morgan recalls having to jump through numerous hoops while constantly striving to deliver his best work.

“And actually, the pressure you put on yourself is too much. When I worked on Guardians of the Galaxy, there were about six Black guys, no Black women on the team. And it was always about making sure our work would speak for itself. And while the external pressure we spoke about earlier gained some traction around 2020 [in the wake of international Black Lives Matter protests following George Floyd’s murder], now it has almost gone the other way around.”

It’s one thing to put characters of color on screen. It’s another to have people from those communities writing their stories and creating the artwork behind the scenes.

Continuing that line of thought, Johnson-Sinclair linked the industry’s retreat from diversity initiatives to broader political developments.

“The regression of historically marginalized people and advocacy for their rights really does coincide with the change of U.S. administration. From my perspective and within organizations, I’ve been working in a setting where the narrative is ‘we can’t do this because we’re scared of repercussions from Donald Trump.’ It’s that explicit. For some organizations, they’ve pivoted into being very quiet about their support, and others have just taken this as the perfect excuse to give up. And because we live in the UK, where a lot of money comes from this industry, it affects us as well.”

When budgets shrink, he continued, major studios make decisions based on their perceptions of which audiences are worth investing in.

“Now, that doesn’t necessarily mean you have to stay within these organizations. I think it’s actually down to us to topple the system, the structures that currently exist, and build around them. Once you have your audience, you can go out there and build something for yourself.”

Finding Your People

Whether someone chooses to navigate the established studio system or pursue a more independent path, Ashton stresses the importance of not doing it alone.

“Finding your community and finding your people is very important, and also understanding where you get that validation, and that you are not alone. A few years ago, there was this global study called We Can’t All Be Lying [launched by the collective It Takes a Village, exploring the experiences of Black women across the creative industries], and it was truly helpful to many of us. In that sense, finding your people can mean a community of writers, animators, whether you do it independently or not. Every choice is valid, and while I personally chose to do things independently, not everybody should be expected to do that. It’s all about finding the way back to yourself while navigating this industry.”

Johnson-Sinclair acknowledges that the process can be difficult and emotionally exhausting.

“When you work in a space where people don’t get it, it can take a toll, and it’s not easy to go back the next day, try to make space for yourself without having to compromise on your identity.”

Morgan similarly emphasizes the value of building relationships and making connections throughout the industry.

“Sadly, the pandemic has killed a lot of the moments when we get to know people by osmosis, and I think a lot of how to get inside this world is just relationship building. Meeting people, making connections, and expanding your network. To me, it’s all about making sure you’re seen, knowing how the game is played, and having access to the right places.”

Access to these networks can be more difficult depending on a person’s cultural, social, and ethnic background, as several studies discussed during the panel illustrated. Ashton also highlighted the importance of mentorship.

“Finding a mentor is also a good way to get help. Someone you can speak to on a regular basis, who understands your issues, and gives you advice.”

Where To Go From Here?

Solidarity is increasingly important at a time when borders around the world are becoming harder to cross. Responding to an audience question, Johnson-Sinclair emphasized the power of associations and grassroots movements.

“What is arguably the most important part of the puzzle is that sometimes, these companies and organizations just need to admit that this work isn’t for them. The best way to start looking might be to partner with people who have actually been doing this forever, rather than try doing it yourself.”

The message was clear: Meaningful change requires more than good intentions. It requires investing in the communities and organizations already doing the work.

Skydance has become the latest, and perhaps loudest, major Hollywood studio to explain how it plans to use AI to cut costs. After its $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery last month, the company is carrying $87 billion in debt and looking to slash expenses.

On Monday, Skydance outlined plans to save at least $6 billion a year within three years, with AI playing a key role in everything from office work and computer programming to film production. “Growing our business and paying down debt are our top priorities,” the company told shareholders.

In a letter to shareholders and subsequent earnings call, executives broke down where the savings will come from:

  • Corporate operations: $2.2 billion. Combining departments, eliminating overlapping jobs, reducing office space, and using AI for administrative work.
  • Technology: $1.4 billion. Combining streaming and computer systems, merging tech teams, and using AI coding tools.
  • Marketing: $1 billion. Combining advertising campaigns and reducing promotional spending.
  • Outside contractors and suppliers: $1.4 billion. Working with fewer vendors and negotiating cheaper contracts.

These are annual savings Skydance expects to achieve within three years, not $6 billion in total cuts. The company hasn’t specified how much AI will contribute or how much it expects to save on labor. Ellison also indicated that potential AI-driven savings in film production aren’t yet included in the company’s forecasts.

What about filmmaking? CEO David Ellison said AI would make production faster and cheaper, while insisting that “artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them.”

At the same time, Ellison predicted that AI could transform filmmaking more dramatically than CGI and digital compositing did in the 1990s, adding that “every discipline across the business will use these tools and productivity will improve as a result.”

Ellison argued that lower production costs could encourage studios to take more risks on original films. But that raises an obvious question for artists: If studios can make the same content faster and cheaper, what happens to the people currently doing that work?

The cuts are already underway. Skydance has offered employee buyouts, and this week confirmed layoffs in its games division, where at least 25 workers have reportedly lost their jobs. On Monday, James Gunn and Peter Safran were also removed as DC Studios chiefs, with Variety reporting that disappointing returns on expensive projects contributed to their ouster.

Skydance hasn’t said which production jobs AI might affect or how many could disappear. But the company’s message to investors is clear: It intends to spend substantially less money running its businesses and producing films and series, and AI is a key driver of how it plans to get there.

After backlash from moviegoers, Laika’s Wildwood is getting a new Spanish-language dub in Mexico. The original drew heavy criticism for using celebrities and social media personalities instead of established voice acting professionals.

Travis Knight’s ambitious stop-motion feature opened in Mexico on October 29, arriving in a country with a tremendous appetite for animated films. But its release quickly sparked controversy over the casting of actress Macarena García as Prue McKeel, influencer and film commentator Javier Ibarreche as the Bandit King, and television personality Natalia Téllez as Alexandra Svik.

Critics argued that the performances lacked the emotional range and expressiveness expected of professional voice actors, creating an unfortunate contrast with the film’s elaborate stop-motion visuals. The backlash spread quickly across social media, inspiring a petition demanding a new dub.

On Tuesday, Mexican distributor Imagem Films Mx announced that it had prepared an alternative version of the film, which will begin screening nationwide on November 12, just two weeks after the original release.

Con ese espíritu, anunciamos una nueva versión de doblaje de Wildwood: El bosque salvaje, que estará disponible en cines de México a partir del 12 de noviembre.

Agradecemos y reconocemos el talento de todas las personas que han dado vida a esta extraordinaria historia.

Los invitamos a descubrir esta aventura creada con tanto arte, dedicación y amor.

#ValoramosTodasLasVoces #ElRespetoNosUne #Wildwood #ElBosqueSalvaje

— Imagem Films Mx (@ImagemFilmsMx) November 10, 2026

In its statement, the company defended the original production, insisting it met established creative and professional standards and received approval from all relevant parties in Latin America.

“The creation of a new version is not intended to invalidate or discredit the previous process, or any of the artistic contributions made,” the distributor said, adding that it welcomed respectful audience feedback and remained committed to considering different perspectives.

According to El País México, the replacement cast includes professional dubbing actors Danna Alcalá and Erica Edwards, while Emilio Treviño will remain in the role of Curtis.

The distributor’s decision is a victory for critics of celebrity voice casting, a common practice in Latin American animation distribution in which distributors hire recognizable personalities for their promotional value rather than their voice-acting credentials. It’s also a rare example of a distributor responding to audience complaints by making a substantial change to a film that’s already in theaters.

Whether the new dub will satisfy those critics remains to be seen, but the controversy has at least given Wildwood a second chance to make a first impression. Perhaps it will even get a second wind at the Mexican box office.

The Forger family is heading back to theaters. Japanese entertainment giant Toho has announced a new Spy x Family feature film for release in Japan in 2027, alongside a fourth season of the mega-hit series, also scheduled to debut next year.

Details about the theatrical feature are still scarce, with Toho yet to reveal a title, plot, director, or production team. The company also hasn’t announced whether the film will receive an international theatrical release, though that seems likely given the franchise’s previous success abroad and anime’s overall popularity in Western cinemas.

This will be the second theatrical production from the franchise, following 2023’s Spy x Family Code: White, which earned more than $60 million at the Japanese box office and received a theatrical release in North America through Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures. Based on Tatsuya Endo’s bestselling manga, Spy x Family debuted in 2022 and follows Loid Forger, a secret agent who assembles a fake family for an undercover mission, unaware that his new wife is an assassin. Their adopted daughter, meanwhile, can read minds and knows both of their secrets.

For all the criticism that Walt Disney Animation Studios (WDAS) has become too reliant on familiar formulas, its fall release, Hexed, is the studio’s fifth animated feature since 2020 built around an original story. The film follows teenage witch Billie Doe (Hailee Steinfeld), who has grown up with suppressed powers and a controlling mother, Alice (Rashida Jones)—not exactly typical Disney fare.

Co-written by studio chief creative officer Jared Bush (Zootopia 2) and Dana Ledoux Miller (Moana 2), and directed by Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand, Hexed is primarily computer-animated, with sequences that are hand-drawn or combine the two techniques. As Billie pushes back against her mother’s rules, she unlocks powers that have lain dormant since birth and is transported to Hexe, a witchy realm where she may truly belong.

“We haven’t had the chance to tell a modern, coming-of-age story, and so that’s really exciting,” Ledoux Miller told Cartoon Brew at a press day in Burbank. “There’s always something that feels so honest and raw about meeting a girl on the cusp of becoming the fullest version of herself. And so, we get to meet this 16-year-old girl who other teenagers can relate to because she’s dealing with the same things in the world as it exists today. But at the same time, there’s this aspirational element of, what if a teenager dealing with a mom who doesn’t understand her woke up one day and found out she had magical powers? What would she do with them? What mistakes would she make? How would she grow as a person? That’s the kind of stuff that we got really excited about, and it hasn’t really been done.”

Cartoon Brew also spoke with the Hexed creative team about the film’s return to hand-drawn animation for its prologue, pushing the limits of CG character animation, and the studio’s ambitions for original animated features.

A Mini Return to Hand-Drawn

Cartoon Brew: WDAS has an established CG animation style, but films like Wish and now Hexed have pushed its boundaries. As directors, where did you want to innovate, and where did you want to draw on the studio’s past?

Fawn Veerasunthorn: The idea of the prologue came upon us wanting to talk about, “Once upon a time in Ohio….” We always let the story lead the discovery, right? The prologue was hand-drawn, combined with the techniques of lighting, so it’s not just straight-up line drawing. What the team had to come up with was quite unique. There’s a bit of glamor. There’s a bit of comedy. There’s a larger-than-life feeling. And as the [Hexed] story progressed, there’s another section of the film that we didn’t show fully today that’s evoking, if you think about the past, what would that sensorial feeling feel like?

Jason Hand: The [prologue’s] shadow idea of light and the moonlight being such a prominent feature in the movie almost has a magic in our movie, as the story will tell you. We liked that idea that you were able to get the story through things being projected with the light, and that felt really interesting to us. Wherever we can push the visual style or the visual storytelling of the movie, we were always looking to do so. There are some other elements in the film where we tried some different stuff that allows everybody in the building to get super excited about trying something different and trying something new. Sometimes that means going back to our roots, which were hand-drawn animation, which we all love so much. At Disney, we’re going backward and forward at the same time. We love to use anything that helps us tell our story in an interesting and really unique way. I love the opening. Once we saw the hand-drawn animation, it’s funny, and it’s really quirky looking. But then the textures of the puppets and the paper were added, and it was really cool. We were excited about how that all feels.

Did you bring back any Disney hand-drawn animation veterans to help on Hexed?

Hand: Ron Clements and John Musker, the legendary film directors, they’re part of our story trust. Ron came in and gave us a lot of really great thoughts on the story specifically. But we have animators from all over, and we have incredible hand-drawn animators. Alex Kupershmidt came on and helped with how the clothing can move. Randy Haycock, who actually animated the magic carpet in Aladdin, helped with the animation and draw-overs. And then Byron Howard, who’s not a throwback because he’s still working, is such an incredible resource for us in entertainment and animation. He is a genuine genius at that, so we use everybody, and we ask for everybody’s help because that’s how we do it here.

Bucket and Beef Rogger

Two of the standout characters in Hexed are Bucket, an anthropomorphic cauldron, and Beef Roger Crummchuk (Walton Goggins), a three-eyed, cat-like witch’s familiar.

Beef Roger has multiple arms and extendable appendages, which present challenges for the rigging team. What makes a character worth the additional work and R&D?

Veerasunthorn: I give the credit to the production team and the whole pipeline who was like, “This seems like a fun character!” Tyler [Mahn] did exploration through hand-drawn just to see where you can push it to the max, and then the team saw it and was like, “Oh, we can do that.” And I’m like, “Really?”

Hand: That’s what we do in animation and this is part of why we get into animation. I remember directly challenging the animators to say, “We want to make Beef Roger a character like we’ve never done in our studio before.” And they’re like, “Sign me up!” They don’t shy away from that. And oftentimes, they actually did more than we ever thought we were ever going to be able to do, and do it in more shots than we ever thought we were going to be able to do. It’s all because of his personality. I think that’s why it goes back to the storyline and why it’s worth it, and that’s why we chose to do it. It was just so much fun.

I think the other aspect is just from a caricature standpoint in general. We really push the proportions of our characters. You can see most obviously in a character like Beef Roger, where we are actually stretching and pushing and pulling him, popping out his eyes. But also it’s in a character like the mother, Alice. We really found this by pushing the caricatured nature of how her limbs work, like maybe would have done back in the past. What it allowed us to do was to have a sense of caricature in the way that they act, the way that they move, but also still gives you the believability that we have for the story that we’re telling, which is this mother-daughter story. So it’s a balance between the two, but we are definitely wanting to push and enjoy doing that for sure.

How did Bucket come about as Billie’s dog-like cauldron companion?

Hand: One of the story artists drew it, and we laughed so hard. Alan Ostergardner pitched that idea, and we were like, “Oh, this is Bucket.” Honestly, that process kind of happens across all of our characters because we are constantly workshopping them. I’m not in theater, but I liken it a little bit to the rehearsal. It’s where you keep working on it and keep workshopping the characters until we all find the things that really connect, and that includes Dana and Jared in the room with us. That’s where that collective story brain really works and can create something super rich. We do get a chance to take a couple of passes at these characters and oftentimes, we can really find some of the magic, or the secret sauce of each character.

Originals, or not?

Original films face pressure to connect with audiences without the benefit of an established franchise. How do you handle that pressure when so much is riding on Hexed?

Veerasunthorn: Jared likes to push things to see where the limit is. He was like, “Don’t be afraid. Just push the comedy really far, push the drama really far, and see where we land.” He never really stopped.

Hand: He was the biggest advocate for this movie, honestly, for all the aspects of it. It is challenging to make an original. We want them to be as good as they possibly can be, and so we will try our hardest to make them the best, the funniest, the most emotional, visually interesting, and different and unique. I think that comes from the top, which is so nice and a luxury for us. And then we just work really hard, and the whole entire team then wants to do the same thing, and that’s exciting.

Jared, how do you give original films the best chance of succeeding in an industry that increasingly favors sequels?

Jared Bush: I’d say the special thing about an original is that no one knows what’s going to happen yet. You’re taking people on this journey. They don’t know the character’s secrets yet. They don’t know whether flaws are flaws or a superpower. They don’t know the worlds that you step into. I watch [movies] with my kids right now, and they want to be surprised by things. They want a new story that takes them to places that they didn’t expect to go. They know all the tropes because they can go online and see every movie ever made, and they know them really, really well. I think for us, it is knowing all those things, and then how do you surprise and delight people? And that’s a really hard thing as we’re moving through the story. But more than anything, people want to go on an emotional roller coaster.

Given animation’s long production timelines, you have to anticipate what audiences will respond to years in advance. How confident do you feel making those decisions two years into your role as CCO?

Bush: I love a learning curve, and it’s constantly that. Regardless of what my role is or what Dana’s role is, the world is continuing to change around us all the time. So, more often than not, we always start with a character. Character is always the thing. But I think beyond that, as you’re moving from movie to movie, it’s how do you tell stories that people will relate to? It always comes down to universal human truths that we hope are timeless. A lot of the stories that we try to tell aren’t stories that will feel topical to this moment right here. Like, [Hexed] is a story about a parent trying to protect their child, and this child wanting to push beyond those protections and those limitations to find her potential. That story exists right now the same way it did 50 years ago. Parents and children will always have that debate, and that’s what this movie is — a debate.

For me personally, as I’m looking at the slate moving forward, 100% we have to tell new original stories. I came to Disney and I had the luxury of working on three originals back to back. It was amazing. But I will also say, I actually do love stepping back into worlds that I help to build with characters that I love. A lot of times people think that there’s a mandate of sequels. Actually, people are excited to jump back into those worlds and spend time with characters that we fell in love with. To me, it is just this balance. And I think a really good balance is a sequel to an original. If we can keep a cadence like that, to me, it makes a lot of sense as we’re moving forward.

And we have the other really fun legacy of musicals, and that’s also another part of this. We have musicals as part of the original continuation story — musical, non-musical — and that’s just a really fun thing. As any creative person, it’s kind of this embarrassment of riches, and every story that we get to tell, we get to jump in and take a vacation in these places. It’s incredibly fulfilling, and it’s really, really fun. Even when the work’s difficult, it’s this really fun puzzle that you’re trying to solve and make the best version that could possibly be.

When it comes to the visual innovation of WDAS features, how do you balance developments at other studios with the capabilities of your own pipeline?

Bush: Sometimes, certainly, as you’re looking at something, you question, “What should this look like?” But usually, the answer to that is, “Why does the story need that?” Anytime you’re pushing style over what the story is, then it’s just different for the sake of being different. A movie we announced called Clay that Fawn is also directing has a very, very different style that makes sense with what that movie is. There’s a reason to really push beyond anything we’ve done before. But there’s so much exciting animation happening around the world beyond the walls of the studio. We are fans of all of it. We are all excited by it. We’re inspired by everything that we see. I think more than anything, as a director in the studio, if you want to push to try something new — fantastic. But make sure that there’s a why, and make sure that style change is going to elevate the film. I think people will see that over the next five to 10 years there’s going to be a lot of that.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Please, written and directed by felt specialist Anna Mantzaris, whose previous shorts include Enough and Good Intentions. Apparat Filmproduktion produced it as a Swedish, French, Czech, Norwegian, and Finnish co-production. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning Best Nordic Short Film at Nordisk Panorama.

Through loosely connected encounters, the film follows people searching for affection, intimacy, and acceptance, often in painfully awkward ways. Mantzaris approaches their neediness with empathy, allowing feelings that self-improvement culture encourages us to suppress to take center stage. Built and shot across three countries, the production also challenged her to direct remotely while developing richer characters and environments without sacrificing the visual simplicity that leaves room for her puppets’ subtle performances.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Anna Mantzaris: I’m interested in how we are as humans, especially our flaws and contradictions, and trying to depict them with distance but at the same time with empathy.

We all want to be loved and feel seen, but so many of us struggle to find this. I was curious to explore how we go about finding love, and how we handle the struggle of not finding it. We live in a society focused on the self, self-improvement, and “becoming our best selves.” But feeling pathetic or needy is part of being human, and I think there is something beautiful about these slightly unwanted sides of us. All of these were themes I felt really drawn to and wanted to explore more.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

This was my first international co-production. With the film being built and shot in three different countries, I did a lot of directing from a distance. I learned that I prefer to be on set, haha. But also how to be clear as a director, how to communicate what I want without being in that room, and how not to lose my vision for the film while also being open to input from my coworkers.

It’s also quite a strange film. It always made sense to me, but I had no idea how people would receive it or if they would get it. The fact that it resonated with so many people has also taught me to trust my gut feeling even more.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Stop motion is my language, so the technique was not a question.

There is something about a more simplified approach, both in characters and in environments, that I’m really drawn to: leaving space for the character to breathe and space for us to see their more subtle acting. I wanted to work in a similar style as I have before, but elevate and improve it, pushing the boundaries of that style. Adding more richness to the world and the characters, while not losing the simplicity and slightly illustrative quality.

Your characters often behave in painfully awkward ways. How did you approach making their neediness uncomfortable without making them unsympathetic?

I think I have a lot of empathy for my characters. Even though they are awkward and very imperfect, I’m not trying to mock them. I’m just trying to portray all the sides of us. I’m interested in the things we feel on the inside but don’t always show to the world, the feelings and urges we are less proud of but can all relate to. In a way, I’m letting the puppets do those things for us. Maybe they are even more true to themselves than we are in certain respects.

Over the weekend, a relatively obscure Instagram account went viral with an AI-generated knockoff of El Empleo, the acclaimed 2008 Argentine animated short that has accumulated millions of views and several top international festival awards over nearly two decades.

The account, Nightframe, has since removed the unauthorized remake after co-creator Patricio Plaza, who directed the short alongside Santiago Bou Grasso, objected to his work being repurposed to promote a paid AI filmmaking service.

The 30-second knockoff reportedly attracted more than five million views in under 24 hours, despite Nightframe having only around 16,000 followers. Neither of the film’s original directors was consulted before its creation or release.

From Plagiarized Short To Paid Subscriptions

The unauthorized remake was obviously problematic, but the commercial connection only became apparent after a closer examination of the Instagram post.

Its caption instructed viewers to “Send AI to find out how I made this film.” Following those instructions triggered an automated private message directing viewers to AI Film School, a service advertising AI filmmaking instruction for $49 per month.

“So these people were not only infringing the film’s copyright, but also using it to make their AI business go viral and generate revenue,” Plaza told us. “I can’t even begin to list all the things that are wrong with this.”

When we reached out, the person behind Nightframe denied profiting from the video or having any financial relationship with AI Film School.

“I’m a student running my Instagram page as a hobby, experimenting with AI filmmaking,” they told us. “I created a 30-second AI interpretation of the original six-minute animation purely for fun, with no intention of exploiting the creator’s work.”

The account operator said the original film had been credited and denied receiving any money from the video or the account.

“I occasionally share AI Film School’s content but have never received any compensation for doing so,” the operator said, adding that the video was removed after Plaza contacted them.

The account did not offer an explanation for why a video supposedly created purely for fun included a prompt that would lead users to an automated promotion for a paid AI filmmaking service.

There’s a bitter irony in the choice of source material for the AI knockoff. El Empleo depicts a world in which human beings are reduced to tools, their labor and bodies exploited for the benefit of others. Nearly two decades later, the film itself has been repurposed without permission to promote technology that promises to automate creative labor, turning years of painstaking artistic work, two years of hand-drawn work on paper in the case of El Empleo, into an advertisement for AI-generated content.

Disney has lined up its next big AI partner, this time teaming with Adobe on a multi-year alliance to bring customized generative AI models into its creative pipelines across its businesses, including tools that will transform hand-drawn sketches into fully rendered concept art.

Under the terms of the agreement, Adobe will be Disney’s official “AI Innovation Partner” and will give the company access to Firefly, Firefly Foundry, Premiere, Photoshop, and dedicated engineering resources. Together, the companies will develop bespoke AI models trained on Disney IP to “generate commercially safe and production-ready outputs.”

According to the release, the work is already underway, with Walt Disney Imagineering using Firefly Foundry to generate 2D concept art from human-made drawings and create IP-based graphics for its parks development. Adobe will also work with Disney’s StudioLAB on experimental production workflows and ESPN Edge on AI-powered sports content.

The Adobe partnership is only the latest in a string of high-profile attempts by Disney to get ahead of the AI curve through corporate partnerships.

A year ago, Disney unveiled its most dramatic overhaul of Disney+ since the streamer’s launch, including a full-on embrace of generative AI tools for users. Then, in December, the company announced a $1 billion investment in OpenAI, a deal that collapsed when Sora was shut down and before any money changed hands.

More recently, Disney hired former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer and committed roughly $180 million to recruiting employees from his former company, as it announced another major round of layoffs in a year largely defined by cuts across the company.

While the financial terms of the Adobe deal have not been made public, such a high-profile partnership once again shows where Disney’s priorities lie. Even as it eliminates thousands of jobs, demands further cost reductions, and commits billions to shareholder-benefiting stock buybacks, the company continues pouring resources into AI technologies that could fundamentally change how creative work is produced, and who gets paid to do it.

The executive shakeup following Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery has reached DC Studios, where James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-presidents after four years. Former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham will take over as president and chief creative officer.

This latest upheaval is particularly surprising given that Gunn and Safran were explicitly included in Skydance’s new leadership team when the merger closed just one month ago. Their departure adds to a broad corporate restructuring that has already seen Warner Bros. film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy leave the company, with Paramount veterans Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein taking their place.

Gunn and Safran were appointed in October 2022 to oversee DC’s film, television, and animation businesses. Gunn was tasked with creative direction while Safran oversaw business and production, with both reporting directly to then-Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav. In a lengthy Instagram post, Gunn acknowledged the difficulties of balancing filmmaking with the responsibilities that came with co-running a major studio, while crediting Safran with shouldering much of that burden:

I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.

Gunn also confirmed that he and Safran remain involved with DC creatively, including an additional project he is currently writing. He also expressed relief at the prospect of returning to filmmaking full-time:

I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking.

Their tenure included an ambitious reboot of DC’s film and television universe, with animation set to play a more interconnected role alongside live-action productions than it had in the past. Gunn’s original vision called for animated projects to share continuity with live-action titles, with actors voicing the same characters they portrayed on screen.

For DC’s animation operations, the leadership change raises fresh questions about the long-term strategy set up by Gunn and Safran. It’s an uncertainty shared across the newly combined Paramount and Warner Bros. businesses, as executives, filmmakers, and employees wait to see how things will shake out.

Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s The Cat in the Hat opened with an estimated $30.5 million worldwide this weekend, including $20.5 million at home, according to Comscore/Rentrak figures.

The latest Dr. Seuss adaptation, directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja, finished second at the domestic box office behind the VFX-heavy monster flick Godzilla Minus Zero, which earned $31.61 million domestically and $63 million worldwide.

The Cat in the Hat opened stronger than many industry outlets had forecast, most expecting a debut in the high teens, but well below previous animated Dr. Seuss adaptations. Universal’s The Lorax opened to $70.2 million in 2012, while Illumination’s The Grinch debuted to $67.5 million in 2018.

A more recent opening-weekend comp is Pixar’s Elio, which opened to $20.8 million before reaching $72.9 million domestically. The key difference here is that The Cat in the Hat carries a considerably smaller budget, reportedly under $90 million compared with Elio’s $150 million-plus price tag. The bar, therefore, is far lower for this colorful kids’ book adaptation, which could also leg out the pre-holiday period thanks to strong word-of-mouth. The film boasts an A CinemaScore and an 81% positive rating from PostTrak respondents.

‘Wildwood’ Holds Strong In Third Weekend

Meanwhile, Travis Knight’s Wildwood continues to boast impressive holding power, earning $7.21 million in its third domestic weekend, down just 20% from its $9.02 million sophomore frame. This comes despite distributor Fathom Entertainment dropping 13% of its theaters in week three, from about 3,100 to 2,693 locations.

After 17 days, Wildwood has grossed around $40.05 million domestically, already surpassing the entire North American theatrical runs of Laika’s Missing Link ($16.6 million) and The Boxtrolls ($17.3 million). The film is also tracking ahead of Kubo and the Two Strings ($48 million) at the same point in its release and looks likely to surpass ParaNorman‘s $56 million domestic total before its time in theaters has passed.

Wildwood finished sixth overall in North America, with a $2,680 per-theater average. Its notably small weekend declines suggest strong word of mouth is sustaining the film’s theatrical run, and plenty of runway ahead.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Paradaïz, the filmmaking debut of Sarajevo-born, Winnipeg-based artist Matea Radic, produced by Jelena Popović for the National Film Board of Canada. Animated entirely on an iPad, the film combines hand-drawn imagery, family photographs, and archival television footage. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning the Golden Dove for short animated film in the international competition at DOK Leipzig.

Returning to Sarajevo for the first time in 25 years, Radic experienced a sudden fear that war might break out again and imagined pulling a hillside over herself like a blanket. That image became the starting point for a surreal exploration of memory, displacement, and belonging. Drawing on childhood recollections of her family’s apartment and an absurdist furniture commercial, she builds a world where familiar surroundings become both hiding places and reminders of what has been lost.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Matea Radic: It was 25 years after having fled Sarajevo that I decided to return for the very first time. As the plane was descending toward the city, I was looking out the window at the rolling hills, and suddenly, a fear came over me. I started to wonder what I would do if the war started again. And in that moment, I imagined myself pulling up the hill as if it were a blanket and hiding underneath it. This image haunted me for some time before I decided to follow myself under that hill and write Paradaïz.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

I learned so much! This was my first film, and I learned something new at every step of the way. One of the biggest lessons was how important it is to have a team to lean on. I was so lucky to have the wonderful people at the NFB supporting me throughout this project. I’m so used to working on my own, but when you spend so much time on a project and become so close to it, having fresh eyes and new perspectives is essential.

I animated the entire film on my iPad, which made for a really streamlined and accessible process. That said, I found myself craving a more analog experience, and I’m excited to explore a more tactile approach in my next project.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I drew heavily on my own childhood memories to build the world of the film. After immigrating to Canada, I became obsessed with drawing the floor plan of our apartment in Sarajevo. I think it was my way of holding on to home, of making sure I wouldn’t forget it. Creating the backgrounds for this film really gave me the chance to put that memory to the test.

I’ve long been interested in the space where the absurd and reality intersect. Through the combination of archival elements and my own animation style, I aimed to explore and bridge these two worlds. The photographs in the film are old family photos, and the commercial is from the ’90s, for a furniture company called Šipad. As a kid, I was obsessed with this commercial because I always wanted to live on the ceiling, and these people were actually doing it.

Did making the film change how you think about your memories of Sarajevo or your idea of home?

It brought me closer to my identity as a Sarajevan. I find myself increasingly drawn to music, literature, and visual art from the former Yugoslavia, exploring a side of my identity I hadn’t connected with before. I’ve always had this little “what if” in the back of my mind about who I might have been had the war never happened, and it’s been meaningful to explore that part of myself. Growing up in the diaspora, I often felt that I was somehow incomplete, but I’ve come to realize the opposite is true. Home isn’t necessarily a place, but rather a feeling of being grounded in yourself.
